slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 10: Favoring Composition and Interface-Based Design. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

slides.narration: The learning target is professional explanation. Learners should be able to say what Favoring Composition and Interface-Based Design changes about program design, not merely identify a keyword. In modern C++, the evidence might be a destructor running, a copy becoming independent, a move leaving ownership in exactly one place, a constrained template rejecting a bad call, or an algorithm producing a predictable sequence.

slides.title: 10.1 Building Objects from Smaller Components
keyPoints: Composition builds behavior from member objects and delegated operations.
Each component owns a focused responsibility: formatting converts a value into text, while a sink accepts the text.
The reporter coordinates them without becoming a subclass of either implementation.
This often reduces coupling because components can change independently while their small contracts remain stable.

slides.title: 10.2.2 Replacing Inheritance with Composition
keyPoints: Replacing inheritance with composition removes the false is-a relationship.
The reporter no longer inherits unrelated destination methods or relies on protected destination state.
Its constructor states exactly which components it requires.
Composition also makes ownership choices explicit.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 10, treat 10.2.2 Replacing Inheritance with Composition as a design decision with costs and evidence. Replacing inheritance with composition removes the false is-a relationship. The reporter no longer inherits unrelated destination methods or relies on protected destination state. Its constructor states exactly which components it requires. Composition also makes ownership choices explicit. A borrowed sink is suitable when an enclosing scope manages several reporters and the destination. An exclusively owned sink may be appropriate when the reporter must determine its lifetime. A shared sink owner is appropriate only when several independent owners genuinely participate in lifetime. Select among those policies deliberately rather than treating one smart-pointer type as a universal interface. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 10, treat Identify the owned value and the borrowed collaborator as a design decision with costs and evidence. The caller creates the memory sink first. The reporter stores its own formatter and a reference to that sink. Two sample calls format the numbers and append the resulting strings. The caller then inspects the sink’s vector. The sink remains alive throughout the reporter’s lifetime, so the reference is valid for every call. The simplest alternative is a reporter that writes directly to std::cout. That can be useful in a tiny program, but it makes exact output tests and destination replacement harder. The explicit sink isolates the dependency without requiring the reporter to understand file paths, terminals, or network connections. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 10, treat Evidence and interpretation as a design decision with costs and evidence. The expected messages are sample=12 and sample=14. slides.title: Failure clinic — A borrowed sink escaped its owner
keyPoints: A helper creates a local memory sink, constructs a reporter that references it, and returns the reporter.
The reporter’s formatter survives by value, but its sink reference dangles as soon as the helper returns.
Copying or moving the reporter does not extend the sink’s lifetime.
The repair is to move destination ownership into the returned object, return both components in a lifetime-safe.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 10, treat Failure clinic — A borrowed sink escaped its owner as a design decision with costs and evidence. A helper creates a local memory sink, constructs a reporter that references it, and returns the reporter. The reporter’s formatter survives by value, but its sink reference dangles as soon as the helper returns. Copying or moving the reporter does not extend the sink’s lifetime. The repair is to move destination ownership into the returned object, return both components in a lifetime-safe arrangement, or require a caller-owned sink that lives long enough. Another defect copies the reporter expecting independent output destinations. Its reference member still designates the same sink. Both copies write into the same vector. That may be a useful shared destination policy, but the documentation and tests should say so. A reference member is not a hidden deep copy of its referent. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 10, treat Review answers and solution notes as a design decision with costs and evidence. The counting sink tests coordination without retaining every message. A throwing sink demonstrates that external failure remains possible; the current reporter propagates it and does not promise rollback of a message already accepted by the destination. Owning a unique sink makes the reporter responsible for its lifetime, while borrowing a sink requires an enclosing owner. Composition eliminates a false inheritance relationship and makes both dependencies visible. The right abstraction is the smallest stable contract the caller actually needs.
